## Claims

### 1. Pastoral frame: comfort, not calendrical prediction
**Claim:** Weima holds that 2 Thess 2:1–17 is the most exegetically difficult Pauline passage, yet Paul’s *overall purpose* is clear: not to predict the future as a prophecy “blueprint,” but to *pastor* a persecuted, frightened church.  
**Quote:** “not to predict the future (contrary to the claims of so-called prophecy experts who approach this passage as a blueprint for spelling out what yet must take place) but to pastor the Thessalonian church.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 3–4; cf. 82–83, 86–87, 203  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`, `paul-apostle`

### 2. Alternate section title
**Claim:** Weima’s alternate title for 2:1–17 is “The Slaying of Satan’s Superman and the Sure Salvation of the Saints: Paul’s Word of Comfort” (citing Weima 2006).  
**Quote:** “The Slaying of Satan’s Superman and the Sure Salvation of the Saints: Paul’s Word of Comfort”  
**Locus:** slice l. 3  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### 3. Five-unit structure of the passage
**Claim:** Weima divides 2:1–17 into five units: (A) crisis 2:1–2; (B) correction 2:3–12; (C) comfort 2:13–14; (D) command 2:15; (E) closing prayer 2:16–17.  
**Quote:** “Paul presents his word of comfort in five discernible units.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 5–15, 85–97, 101–133  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### 4. Passage extent to v. 17 (not stop at v. 12)
**Claim:** Weima argues against majority practice of ending the unit at 2:12 (commentators and NA28/UBS paragraphing); the unit must run through 2:17 because only then does the passage close on *comfort*, not judgment.  
**Quote:** “If one reads only up to verse 12, the passage closes with a note of judgment for unbelievers. … If, however, one reads all the way to verse 17, the passage closes with a note of comfort for the Thessalonian Christians.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 41–83, 425–427  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `jeffrey-weima`

### 5. Inclusio and links binding 2:1–12 to 2:13–17
**Claim:** Weima lists verbal/thematic inclusio and contrasts: v. 2 // v. 15 (word/letter; omission of “spirit” significant); mental instability (v. 2) // stand firm + strengthen (vv. 15, 17); truth/lie and destruction/salvation contrasts between unbelievers (3–12) and believers (13–17); structural parallel with 1 Thess 2:17–4:1.  
**Quote:** “There is a verbal inclusio between verse 2 … and verse 15 … The omission of the first prepositional phrase in v. 15 is significant.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 45–79  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`

### 6. Apocalyptic style with restraint
**Claim:** Weima affirms use of apocalyptic images/themes (esp. vv. 3–12) but resists calling the whole of 2:1–17 full-blown apocalypse; restraint in applying the label is required.  
**Quote:** “The apostle does employ images and themes that are similarly found in apocalyptic writings of his day, but he does so only in one section of this passage (vv. 3–12) and not to the same degree as is found in true apocalyptic texts.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 21–22  
**Pages:** `apocalyptic-literature`, `2-thessalonians`

### 7. Whisper where Scripture whispers
**Claim:** Weima’s interpretive principle for this obscure text: shout where Scripture is frequent/clear; whisper where infrequent/unclear—yet the *comfort* purpose must be shouted.  
**Quote:** “there are many subjects that the Bible addresses frequently and with great clarity, and these are the things that the exegete ought to shout. But there are some subjects that the Bible addresses infrequently and with less clarity, and these are the things that the exegete ought to whisper.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 25–27  
**Pages:** `jeffrey-weima`, `2-thessalonians`

### 8. Crisis: false claim that the day of the Lord has come
**Claim:** The crisis is a false claim that “the day of the Lord has come,” which has shaken and alarmed a young church already apprehensive about eschatological fate (cf. 1 Thess 5:1–11).  
**Quote:** “claiming that the day of the Lord has come”; “scared out of their wits, fearful of whether they would avoid the wrath of God connected with the day of judgment and instead experience salvation.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 5–6, 139, 149–150, 167–180  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`

### 9. Perfect tense *enestēken* = presence, not mere imminence
**Claim:** Weima rejects “is at hand / just at hand” for *enestēken*; the perfect means the day *has come* (presence). Reasons include: Pauline use of *enistēmi* for present realities; Paul’s own agreement that the day is near (so he would not warn against *imminence*); correction in 3–12 targets *presence* claim.  
**Quote:** “the vast majority of Bible translations and commentators render the false claim … as ‘the day of the Lord has come.’”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 169–172  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`

### 10. Why the claim could frighten: complex day + OT judgment stress
**Claim:** Most commentators (Weima following) explain Thessalonian fear by taking “day of the Lord” as a complex of events (parousia one part); the claim would mean that series has begun. Fear attaches more to *day of the Lord* (OT judgment stress) than to the eagerly awaited parousia.  
**Quote:** “the claim that ‘the day of the Lord has come,’ therefore, would be interpreted by the Thessalonians to mean that the series of events connected with that eschatological day have begun to unfold.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 173–179  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`

### 11. Source triad: spirit / word / letter — Paul suspects prophecy
**Claim:** Paul lists three possible media—“through a prophetic utterance or through a spoken word or through a written letter”—suggesting uncertainty, but Weima (with majority) holds Paul *suspects* a Spirit-inspired prophecy (*pneuma*); v. 15 affirms word and letter while *omitting* spirit.  
**Quote:** “he suspects the guilty member of the triad to be the first one mentioned: the Spirit, or … ‘spiritual/prophetic utterance’”; “What is conspicuously missing in this instance … is the first member of the former triad, ‘through the Spirit.’”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 183–188, 486–487  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`

### 12. “*hōs di’ hēmōn*” not a forged letter “from us”
**Claim:** Weima rejects reading “supposedly through us” as only a forged letter *from* Paul (contra Bruce, Witherington, et al. on 3:17). *Dia* marks instrumentality not source (*apo*); v. 15’s hold-to-letter command would be odd if the error came via forged letter; phrase most likely modifies all three triad members—error *attributed* to Paul.  
**Quote:** “the apostle is not referring to a counterfeit letter claiming to come ‘from us’ but rather to a genuine Pauline letter that has been misinterpreted … mediated ‘through us.’”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 191–195  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `paul-apostle`

### 13. Sequence prerequisite: apostasy + man of lawlessness before day of Lord
**Claim:** Correction: day of Lord will not come *unless* the apostasy comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed (incomplete conditional; apodosis supplied: “that day will not come”).  
**Quote:** “that day will not come unless the apostasy comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 141, 211–217  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `antichrist`

### 14. Future–present alternation, not timetable
**Claim:** Weima (with Marshall) notes Paul alternates future (3–5; 8–10) and present (6–7; 11–12) rather than chronological order; not a “timetable of apocalyptic events” for prophecy experts but proof the day is not present.  
**Quote:** “Paul is not interested in spelling out a detailed ‘timetable of apocalyptic events’ … but rather in proving to the Thessalonians that the claim about the day of the Lord being present cannot be true.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 201–203  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `apocalyptic-literature`, `jeffrey-weima`

### 15. Elliptical shorthand due to prior teaching
**Claim:** Readers “walk into the middle of a conversation”; prior oral teaching (imperfect *elegon* “I was repeatedly saying,” v. 5; cf. 1 Thess 5:1–2) allows Paul to speak in elliptical “shorthand” the Thessalonians understood but moderns do not.  
**Quote:** “The modern reader of 2 Thess. 2, therefore, is walking into the middle of a conversation between Paul and the Thessalonian believers.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 197–201, 305–307  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`

### 16. Apostasy primarily religious rebellion (with possible political spillover)
**Claim:** *Apostasia* for Weima is primarily religious rebellion against God (failure to receive gospel truth; worship of pseudo-god), though political/civil dimensions need not be excluded; Second Temple and NT backgrounds of end-time falling away are surveyed.  
**Quote:** “‘the apostasy’ mentioned by Paul here in 2:3 likely refers to a rebellion against God, which is primarily religious in nature.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 219–226  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `apocalyptic-literature`

### 17. Participants in apostasy: humankind broadly, not Jews-only or large-scale Christian defection
**Claim:** Weima rejects Best’s Jewish-rejection view and is unconvinced that apostasy is primarily large-scale Christian defection; prefers Morris’s “rebellion of the creature against the Creator,” including outward associates of the people of God who cannot withstand the lawless one’s deceptive signs.  
**Quote:** “It may be best, therefore, to see in the term *apostasia* more generally ‘the rebellion of the creature against the Creator’ (Morris 1991: 219n18).”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 227–229  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`

### 18. Man of lawlessness = Satan’s servant, not Satan; parallel to Johannine antichrist with temporal nuance
**Claim:** The man of lawlessness is not Satan (v. 9) but “Satan’s superman”; typically identified with John’s “antichrist,” yet Paul targets a future individual before the day of Lord, while John addresses present deniers; Weima sees no fundamental conflict (John leaves room for future personal antichrist; Paul sees lawlessness already at work).  
**Quote:** “This figure is not Satan himself, as verse 9 makes clear, but is the servant of Satan, or in colloquial terms, ‘Satan’s superman.’”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 233–234  
**Pages:** `antichrist`, `2-thessalonians`

### 19. Titles: “man of lawlessness” / “son of destruction”
**Claim:** Semitic idioms: personification of lawlessness (*anomia* as broad rebellion against God, not mere Mosaic antinomianism); “son of destruction” = *doomed to destruction* (intransitive *apōleia*), foreshadowing v. 8 and followers’ fate (v. 10)—consolatory.  
**Quote:** “the second title refers to the lawless one’s ultimate destiny: he is the one ‘doomed to destruction.’”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 235–244  
**Pages:** `antichrist`, `2-thessalonians`

### 20. Opposes and exalts; sits in temple proclaiming he is God
**Claim:** Man of lawlessness “opposes and exalts himself over every being called god or every object of worship,” so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself God; *naos* (inner sanctuary, not *hieron*); formal public self-deification (*apodeiknymi*). Closest parallels: Dan 11:36; 12:10; Antiochus / Pompey / Caligula pattern.  
**Quote:** “so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming that he himself is God.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 141, 245–260, 281–290  
**Pages:** `antichrist`, `eschatological-temple`, `2-thessalonians`

### 21. “Temple of God” = Jerusalem temple (metaphorically typological), not heavenly temple or church
**Claim:** Weima rejects (a) heavenly temple and (b) church-as-temple (Chrysostom, Reformers vs papacy, Giblin, Beale). Prefers historic Jerusalem temple *metaphorically/typologically*: graphic desecration motif for usurpation of God’s authority; “says more about the character of the man of lawlessness than the location where he will make his appearance.” Not a requirement to rebuild a future literal temple for prediction fulfillment (contra Thomas; Hippolytus/Cyril lineage noted).  
**Quote:** “It may be best to conclude that the Jerusalem sanctuary is meant here by Paul and his companions, but meant in a metaphorical sense.” (Bruce, endorsed); “Taking up a motif derived from Ezekiel and Daniel … he has used this language to portray the character of the culminating manifestation of evil.” (Marshall, endorsed)  
**Locus:** slice ll. 261–297  
**Pages:** `eschatological-temple`, `antichrist`, `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`

### 22. Pre-70 authorship implication of temple reference (via Caligula “close call”)
**Claim:** Weima notes Caligula’s AD 40 plan to set his statue in the Jerusalem temple as a “close call” ~11–12 years before 2 Thessalonians, keeping temple-desecration expectation alive—material that situates the letter while the temple stood and informs the historical texture of the temple motif (without Weima treating temple alone as a full authorship proof).  
**Quote:** “Another well-known desecration—or more accurately, potential desecration—of the Jerusalem temple occurred just over a decade before the writing of Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians. In AD 40 the emperor Caligula …”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 287–289; cf. Excursus objection to Rome view, l. 604  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `eschatological-temple`, `paul-apostle`

### 23. Mild rebuke in 2:5; singular “I”
**Claim:** Rhetorical *ou* + imperfect *elegon* = mild rebuke: they *do* remember repeated teaching. Shift plural→singular stresses Paul’s personal role; literary (not literal) “we” with Silas/Timothy. Reference to oral mission teaching rather than 1 Thess does not support pseudepigraphy (Trilling) or 2 Thess-before-1 (Wanamaker)—different problem than 4:13–5:11.  
**Quote:** “You remember, don’t you, that when I was still with you, I was repeatedly saying these things to you?”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 301–315  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `2-thessalonians-authorship`, `paul-apostle`

### 24. Mystery of lawlessness already at work
**Claim:** “Mystery of lawlessness” is Pauline ad hoc: *mystērion* = divine truth once hidden, now revealed (not pagan mystery cult); lawlessness already operative but limited by the restrainer until removal; then man of lawlessness revealed at his fixed time (God’s sovereignty over *kairos*).  
**Quote:** “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work only until the one who is now restraining is out of the way.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 141, 330–338  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `antichrist`, `apocalyptic-literature`

### 25. Neuter *to katechon* / masculine *ho katechōn* pair
**Claim:** Restraint described both impersonally (neuter, v. 6) and personally (masculine, v. 7); any identification must fit both. Parallel: lawlessness as mystery (impersonal) and man (personal). Both restraining forms are *present*.  
**Quote:** “the restraining activity is described both impersonally with the neuter *to katechon* … and personally with the masculine *ho katechōn*.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 317–318, 566–568  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `2-thessalonians`

### 26. *Katechō* means “restrain/hold back” (positive)
**Claim:** Weima argues from context (esp. *monon … heōs*), common NT/Pauline sense, extrabiblical use, fathers (Tertullian, Chrysostom), and Jewish “delaying” end-time factors under God that *katechō* here = restrain/hinder; consensus of major translations and commentators that the influence is positive/beneficial.  
**Quote:** “the most plausible conclusion is that its two occurrences here convey the notion of holding back or hindering.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 570–578  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`

### 27. Rejected senses of *katechō*: “hold sway” and “seize/possess”
**Claim:** Weima rejects intransitive “hold sway/rule” (Robinson, Frame, Vos, Best, Weatherly—evil supportive force) as lacking NT parallels and as transitive in context with lawless one as implied object. Rejects Giblin’s “seize/possess” (false prophet/demonic seizure; Green on cult possession) as rare, non-Pauline, and cosmically implausible if end depends on removing one local false prophet.  
**Quote:** “That Paul believed the coming of Christ would or could be held up until some local false prophet was out of the way seems highly unlikely.” (Wanamaker, endorsed)  
**Locus:** slice ll. 574–576, 620–621  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`

### 28. Surveyed identification proposals (1–6) as attributed options
**Claim:** Weima surveys seven proposals; options 1–6 are recorded as positions he evaluates and finds wanting:

1. **Roman Empire + emperor** (Tertullian, Hippolytus; once majority)—objections: Paul’s sufferings under Rome; anti-imperial notes (1 Thess 5:3); Jewish/Christian oracles portray Rome as enemy; Caligula resembles lawless one; lawlessness primarily religious; Rome now “out of the way” without apostasy/man of lawlessness appearing. Variant: Rome as *evil* preparatory force via intransitive *katechō*—rejected grammatically/contextually.  
2. **Law and order + political leaders generally**—same critiques; singular more naturally one known individual.  
3. **Gospel proclamation + Paul** (Justin, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret, Calvin; Cullmann, Munck; Beale notes gospel side)—“fatal” flaw: Paul expected to live till parousia (1 Thess 4:15, 17); “out of the way” odd for own death; cosmic role of one ministry dubious; death did not usher in lawless one. Modification to generic “preacher” weakened by masculine singular.  
4. **Church + Holy Spirit / rapture** (dispensationalist: English, Scofield, Walvoord, Thomas, Powell)—rapture of Spirit with church hard to defend (cf. 1 Thess 4:17 comments); Paul names Holy Spirit explicitly at 2:13; Spirit as God cannot be “out of the way.”  
5. **Power of evil + Satan** (Frame, Dixon, Best)—depends on rejected intransitive reading; Satan exiting to make room for lawless one improbable given parousia “in conformity with the work of Satan” (2:9).  
6. **False prophecy + false prophet** (Giblin; Green)—objections already under sense of *katechō*.  

**Locus:** slice ll. 587–621  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `principalities-powers`, `paul-apostle`, `2-thessalonians`

### 29. Weima’s preferred identification: archangel Michael (Daniel 10–12)
**Claim:** Weima’s preferred solution: neuter = restraining *activity* of Michael; masculine = Michael *as person*. Allusions: man of lawlessness // Dan 12:10; self-exaltation/temple // Dan 11:31, 36; restrainer // Michael in Dan 10–12. Paul emphasizes *function* (restraint) not name because readers already know identity; sequence answers fear that day has come.  
**Quote:** “the neuter attributive participle in verse 6 focuses on the restraining activity of the archangel Michael, and the masculine attributive participle in verse 7 has in view the archangel Michael as a person.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 342–346, 622–627  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `principalities-powers`, `apocalyptic-literature`, `jeffrey-weima`

### 30. Daniel 10–12 chronological schema paralleled
**Claim:** Weima (via Hannah 2000; Nicholl 2004; also Witherington, Shogren) maps fourfold parallel:

| Dan 10–12 | 2 Thess 2 |
|---|---|
| Michael currently restrains evil (10:20–11:45) | “now restraining” (2:6a, 7a) |
| Michael “stands/stands aside” (12:1a MT/LXX *parerchomai*) | “until he is out of the way” (2:7b) |
| Unequaled distress (12:1b) | Apostasy + revelation of lawless one (2:3–4, 8–10) |
| Deliverance + judgment (12:1c–3) | Day of Lord: destroy lawless one & followers; save/glorify believers (2:3–14) |

**Quote:** “The chronological schema in Dan. 10–12, therefore, parallels exactly that followed by Paul in 2 Thess. 2:3–12.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 625–634  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `principalities-powers`, `apocalyptic-literature`

### 31. “Out of the way” = fact of removal, not manner
**Claim:** *Ek mesou genētai*: subject is the restrainer; fact of removal, not whether voluntary or violent (contra Fulford voluntary; Dobschütz violent). Later magical papyrus (PGM 4.2770) calls Michael *katechōn* of the great dragon—late but shows Michael known as restrainer.  
**Quote:** “The fact, not the manner, of removal is indicated” (Frame, endorsed).  
**Locus:** slice ll. 340–341, 637–638  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`

### 32. Angelic restrainer background beyond Michael
**Claim:** Supporting angelic restraint motifs: Rev 20:1–3 (bind Satan); Rev 7:1 (four angels hold winds); 1 En. 10 (Raphael/Michael bind watchers). God cannot be restrainer because God cannot be “out of the way.” Paul already links angels to parousia (2 Thess 1:7; 1 Thess 4:16).  
**Quote:** “Although one might naturally think of God as playing the role of the restrainer, this possibility has to be rejected on the grounds that it is impossible for God to disappear from the scene.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 622–623  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `principalities-powers`

### 33. Whisper still required on restrainer

### 34. Two parousias; Christ slays lawless one by breath of mouth (Isa 11:4)
**Claim:** After restrainer’s removal, “then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and will destroy by the sudden appearance of his coming.” Illogical order (destruction before describing lawless one’s coming) is *pastoral*—comfort first. Allusion to Isa 11:4 LXX; breath = potent war weapon, not “little word” lightly felling (contra Luther hymn reading as Weima frames it). *Katargeō* ≈ destroy/annihilate (synonymous parallelism). *Epiphaneia* stresses sudden Hellenistic manifestation of a deity.  
**Quote:** “whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and will destroy by the sudden appearance of his coming.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 141, 349–367  
**Pages:** `antichrist`, `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`

**Quote:** “precisely because his signs and wonders are real, they are so dangerous.”

Rom 1:25), not primarily future claim of v. 4 or wonders of v. 9. Result: all who have not believed the truth but delighted in wickedness will be condemned (final judgment; cf. 1:6, 9).

### 39. Comfort unit: election and calling guarantee salvation
**Claim:** 2:13–14: thanksgiving (echoing 1:3 with intensified “we,” *de*, reordered obligation, “brothers loved by the Lord”) because God *chose* them as *firstfruits* for salvation through sanctifying work of the Spirit and belief in the truth, and *called* them through “our gospel” for obtaining the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ. Contrast with perishing unbelievers.  
**Quote:** “God chose you as firstfruits for salvation by means of the sanctifying work of the Spirit and your belief in the truth. … he also called you through our gospel for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### 40. Text-critical preference: *aparchēn* “firstfruits” over *ap’ archēs* “from the beginning”
**Claim:** Weima (with Metzger, Fee) prefers “firstfruits” on internal grounds (Pauline usage; copyist tendency to change *aparchēn* elsewhere); comforts small persecuted church as vanguard of eschatological harvest in Thessalonica (and quality nuance possible).

### 41. “Loved by the Lord” = Jesus; church as renewed Israel
**Claim:** *Kyrios* = Jesus (not God); possible deliberate contrast with antichrist’s followers; phrase echoes Deut 33:12 LXX (Benjamin blessing applied to Gentile converts); Israel-language reapplied → church as renewed Israel of God (Weima 1996).

**Locus:** slice ll. 440–446  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`, `jeffrey-weima`

### 42. Command: stand firm and hold the traditions (word/letter)
**Claim:** 2:15 *ara oun*: stand firm *by* holding fast the traditions taught either by word (mission oral teaching) or letter (1 Thessalonians); inclusio with 2:2 omitting *pneuma*; test of prophecy = agreement with Paul’s oral/written traditions (cf. 1 Thess 5:19–22). Only imperatives in 2:1–17.  
**Quote:** “So then, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught either by our word or by our letter.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 145, 474–487  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`

### 43. Closing prayer: eternal comfort + strengthen for work/word
**Claim:** Double-petition prayer (optative): Christ and God (singular verbs with two subjects—equal honor without merging persons) comfort hearts; God described as giver of “eternal comfort and good hope by his grace.” Second petition “strengthen … in every good work and word” transitions to ch. 3 idle/work problem (parallel 1 Thess 3:11–13 foreshadowing). Comfort ultimately divine, not merely human obedience to v. 15.  
**Quote:** “the prayer highlights what Christ himself and God will do. The comfort available to the shaken believers … rests ultimately not on their human ability to obey the command … but on the divine activity of both Christ and God.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 489–517  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `paul-apostle`

### 44. God sovereign over revelation of lawless one
**Claim:** Thrice-passive *apokalyptō* (vv. 3, 6, 8): God (unspoken agent) controls when restraint ends and lawless one is revealed—through angelic agency of Michael. Comfort: future under God’s control.  
**Quote:** “Since God is the one who, through the angelic agency of Michael, is currently restraining lawlessness, it logically follows that he also is the one who determines when that restraint will end.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 351–352  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `principalities-powers`, `2-thessalonians`

### 45. Related problems in letter (suffering; idlers) linked to 2:1–17 crisis
**Claim:** Weima notes unjust suffering (1:3–12) and rebellious idlers (3:1–15) are “almost certainly … connected with the problem taken up here in 2:1–17.”  
**Quote:** “the other subjects taken up in the letter … almost certainly are connected with the problem taken up here in 2:1–17.”  
**Locus:** slice l. 150  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### 46. Text-critical notes of load-bearing interest
**Claim:** Weima prefers: “man of lawlessness” over “man of sin” (v. 3; *anomia* in 7–8); omits later “as God” before “takes his seat” (v. 4); includes “Jesus” with *kyrios* in v. 8 (brackets); *anelei* “will slay” as original Isa 11:4 assimilation; present *pempei* not future *pempsei* (v. 11).  
**Locus:** slice ll. 519–540  
**Pages:** `2-thessalonians`, `antichrist`, `weima-1-2-thessalonians-becnt`

### 47. Ridderbos non-specific apocalyptic reading registered and declined
**Claim:** Weima records Ridderbos’s view that one should not identify the restrainer with specific historic phenomena (apocalyptic language of supernatural factors) but rejects abandoning identification: Paul says the Thessalonians *know* the entity from prior teaching; apocalyptic symbols are “seldom nonreferential” (Witherington).  
**Quote:** “Apocalyptic symbols and terminology are often deliberately vague so they may be multivalent, but they are seldom nonreferential.”  
**Locus:** slice ll. 581–583  
**Pages:** `restrainer-2-thess-2`, `apocalyptic-literature`

## What this slice does *not* decide (Weima’s own restraint)
- Exact chronology between apostasy and revelation of the lawless one (grammar ambiguous; not a timetable).  
- Precise manner of restrainer’s removal.  
- Whether temple motif requires a rebuilt future Jerusalem temple (Weima: metaphorical/typological use of historic temple motif).  
- Full resolution of authorship of 2 Thessalonians (oral-teaching argument against Trilling/Wanamaker is local; Caligula chronology situates but is not a full authorship treatise).
